Distributed practice�involves a type of learning schedule in which sessions are separated by a rest period.�

Distributed practice is most useful when the learner must make use of physical skills or motor skills. Distributed practice allows the individual to master learning in a small area of a skill.This gives confidence and motivation to conquer another area of skills in a subsequent distributed practice.

For example, when a musician is learning a difficult piece, he will practice one section of the music over and over again until he is familiar and comfortable with it before attempting the next section.

One disadvantage�may be that forgetting of previously learned material will sometimes occur between sessions.�

This is why teachers often spend the first few minutes of class reviewing the material covered the day before.

Research suggests that distributed practice is very effective in helping students retain and recall knowledge. By letting some time go by and then revisiting the same information, our brains will hold onto the information for longer.

For example:�If you need to study for 3 hours, it's more effective to study for 30 minutes every night for 6 days than to try and study for 3 hours all at once.�
